references.text: In the preceding verse ([ref:Luk 16:25|Luke 16:25]), Abraham explains that Lazarus is now comforted while the rich man is tormented—the irreversible reversal of their earthly conditions forms the basis for the great chasm described in verse 26.

In [ref:Jes 35:8|Isaiah 35:8], a holy way is spoken of that the unclean shall not walk on. The idea of an insurmountable dividing line between the righteous and the wicked echoes the great chasm in Luke 16:26.

[ref:Matt 25:46|Matthew 25:46] speaks of eternal punishment for the wicked and eternal life for the righteous. The final and irreversible separation between these two groups parallels the fixed chasm between the rich man and Lazarus.

[ref:Matt 25:41|Matthew 25:41] describes the judgment where the cursed are sent away into eternal fire. This final separation corresponds to the insurmountable chasm established between the saved and the lost.

In [ref:Åp 20:11-15|Revelation 20:11–15], the final judgment at the great white throne is depicted, where those not written in the book of life are cast into the lake of fire. The permanent separation between the saved and the lost mirrors the fixed chasm in Luke 16:26.

In [ref:Luk 13:24-25|Luke 13:24–25], Jesus speaks of the narrow door that is shut, so that those who knock can no longer enter. This irreversible exclusion is a thematic parallel to the chasm that prevents any crossing.

[ref:Fork 11:3|Ecclesiastes 11:3] says that wherever the tree falls, there it lies. The image is used to express that the state after death is final and unchangeable—something echoed in the fixed chasm between Abraham and the rich man.
[ref:Hebr 9:27|Hebrews 9:27] states that it is appointed for people to die once, and after that comes judgment. The final judgment after death is the basis for the insurmountable chasm in Luke 16:26.

[ref:2 Pet 2:4|2 Peter 2:4] mentions angels who sinned and were kept in chains of darkness until judgment. The image of an inevitable captivity awaiting judgment parallels the irreversible separation represented by the great chasm.

[ref:Matt 7:13-14|Matthew 7:13–14] speaks of the narrow and the wide gate that lead respectively to life and destruction. The two paths that never meet reflect the absolute separation between the saved and the lost in Luke 16:26.
